title: Stay like a local
headline: Sleep, eat and live among Italians
tagline: Farm stays, scattered village hotels, cave rooms, monastery cells, mountain huts and home-cooked dinners: the ways to swap a hotel lobby for real Italian life.

hero_image.alt: A stone farmhouse agriturismo with a pool among vineyards and cypresses near Montepulciano
hero_image.credit: Walter Giannetti, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: Where you sleep shapes the Italy you see. In a city-centre hotel you meet other travellers; on a working farm you meet the family who pressed the oil on your table, and in a village apartment you learn the rhythm of the bakery queue and the evening stroll. Italy has unusually good options for this, many of them protected by law and run by people who are proud of their place.

Below are the main ways to stay with and among locals, with real examples and the official networks to book through, from farm-stay portals to the association of scattered village hotels. Most cost no more than a mid-range hotel, and many cost less. At the end you will find our short guide to blending in, because a few small courtesies, a greeting at the door or knowing when lunch happens, go a long way.

sections.heading: Stay on a farm
sections.intro: Italy's rural stays are rooted in working agriculture, and the best ones feed you from their own land.

items.title: Agriturismi
items.subtitle: Farm stays, all over Italy
items.desc: An agriturismo is, by law, a working farm that hosts guests, so the wine, oil, cheese or vegetables at dinner usually come from a few metres away. Many serve a set farmhouse dinner that is the highlight of the day. Look for them through the big farmers' associations as well as the main portal: Agriturist, Terranostra and Coldiretti's Campagna Amica, which also lists farm shops and farmers' markets.
items.meta: From about €70 a night for two, often with breakfast

image.alt: An olive grove on a hillside above the blue water of Lake Garda
image.credit: Mario GardaGarda, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Masserie in Puglia
items.subtitle: Fortified farmhouses of the south
items.desc: Puglia's masserie are whitewashed farm estates, many with defensive towers built against pirate raids, set among ancient olive trees. Some are still working farms with a handful of rooms; others, like Masseria Moroseta near Ostuni or the grand Masseria Torre Maizza, have become design hotels. Either way, expect long lunches under a pergola and olive oil from the estate.
items.meta: Best in May to June and September

image.alt: The whitewashed courtyard of Masseria Triglie, a fortified farmhouse near Crispiano in Puglia
image.credit: FrDr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Alpine farm holidays
items.subtitle: Roter Hahn / Gallo Rosso, South Tyrol
items.desc: In South Tyrol, more than a thousand mountain farms (masi, or Höfe) take guests under the Roter Hahn (Red Rooster) quality mark. Children feed the animals, breakfasts come with farm butter and speck, and many farms sell their own juice, cheese and schnapps. It is one of the friendliest ways to see the Dolomites.
items.meta: Rooms and apartments, summer and winter

image.alt: Meadows and a farmhouse below the Odle peaks in Val di Funes, South Tyrol
image.credit: Wolfgang Moroder, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Sleep somewhere with a story
sections.intro: Historic buildings brought back to life by people who live there. These are often the most memorable nights of a trip.

items.title: Alberghi diffusi
items.subtitle: A hotel spread across a village
items.desc: An idea born in Friuli after the 1976 earthquake to revive emptying villages: one reception in the square, with rooms scattered among restored houses. Sauris in Friuli was among the first; the most celebrated is Sextantio in Santo Stefano di Sessanio, Abruzzo; Corte Fiorita in Bosa, Sardinia, is another favourite.
items.meta: You live in the village, not beside it

image.alt: Wooden chalets of Sauris di Sopra among meadows and mountains in Friuli
image.credit: Mattana, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Cave rooms in the Sassi
items.subtitle: Matera, Basilicata
items.desc: Matera's cave districts were evacuated in the 1950s and are now a UNESCO site full of restored cave homes. Sextantio's Le Grotte della Civita keeps them candlelit and almost bare; many family-run B&Bs offer cosier versions. Waking up inside the rock is unforgettable.
items.meta: Book ahead for spring and autumn weekends

image.alt: The cave houses of Matera's Sassi stacked below the cathedral bell tower
image.credit: Bönisch, CC BY-SA 2.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Trulli
items.subtitle: Valle d'Itria, Puglia
items.desc: The cone-roofed stone houses of the Valle d'Itria are built without mortar, cool in summer and snug in winter. Stay in one in Alberobello's old quarter, or better, in the countryside between Locorotondo, Cisternino and Martina Franca, where trulli sit among vineyards and dry-stone walls.
items.meta: Look for countryside trulli with a pool

image.alt: Conical stone roofs and whitewashed walls of trulli in Alberobello
image.credit: Giorgio Galeotti, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Monastery and convent stays
items.subtitle: Guest houses run by religious orders
items.desc: Hundreds of monasteries and convents welcome guests of any faith, from simple rooms near the Vatican to hilltop abbeys in Tuscany and Umbria. Expect peace, spotless rooms, fair prices and sometimes a curfew. Monasterystays.com books a large selection in English.

image.alt: The brick bell tower and church of the Abbey of Monte Oliveto Maggiore among cypresses
image.credit: Adrian Michael, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Mountain rifugi
items.subtitle: Huts in the Alps and Apennines
items.desc: Rifugi are staffed mountain huts, many owned by the Club Alpino Italiano (CAI), offering bunks or simple rooms with half board. Dinner with hikers from all over Europe, then sunrise over the peaks, is a rite of passage. Most open from about mid-June to late September; book early.
items.meta: Bring a sleeping-bag liner and cash

image.alt: Rifugio Locatelli and its chapel below the Tre Cime di Lavaredo in the Dolomites
image.credit: Je-str, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Live among locals
sections.intro: For a week or more, a home in a residential neighbourhood beats any hotel.

items.title: Family-run B&Bs
items.subtitle: A room in someone's home or building
items.desc: Italian B&Bs are usually small, with a host who will tell you where they eat and which bakery opens first. They are especially good value in the south and in smaller cities like Lecce, Siracusa and Bologna. Expect a sweet breakfast: cornetto, cake, coffee.
items.meta: Breakfast is typically sweet, not cooked

image.alt: Aerial view of the island of Ortigia, the old centre of Syracuse, surrounded by deep blue sea
image.credit: Agostino Artnoir Sella, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Apartments in residential neighbourhoods
items.subtitle: Airbnb, Booking.com and local agencies
items.desc: Choose a lived-in district a short ride from the sights, such as Testaccio or Pigneto in Rome, Bolognina in Bologna or Vomero in Naples, and shop at the local market. Every legal short-term rental in Italy must display a national CIN code on its listing and at the door; skip listings without one.
items.meta: Have your passport ready at check-in

image.alt: A long brick-columned portico along Strada Maggiore in Bologna
image.credit: Giovanni Osbat, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: House swaps and house-sitting
items.subtitle: HomeExchange, HomeLink, TrustedHousesitters
items.desc: Swap your home for one in Italy, or look after someone's house and pets in return for free accommodation. Swappers tend to leave notes on the best local trattoria and the neighbours to say hello to, which is half the joy.
items.meta: Membership fees apply; plan months ahead

image.alt: A lakeside lane of pastel houses and café tables in Peschiera Maraglio on Monte Isola
image.credit: CristianNX, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: WWOOF Italia
items.subtitle: Volunteering on organic farms
items.desc: Join WWOOF Italia and you can stay with organic farmers, working a few hours a day in exchange for food and a bed. Help with the grape harvest in autumn or the olive harvest in November, learn to make cheese, and eat with the family.
items.meta: Annual membership; you arrange stays with hosts directly

image.alt: Gathering olives in nets beneath olive trees during the harvest in Tuscany
image.credit: PROPOLI87, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Eat at a local's table
sections.intro: If you cannot stay with Italians, you can still eat with them.

items.title: Le Cesarine
items.subtitle: Home cooks across Italy
items.desc: Founded in Bologna in 2004 to protect regional home cooking, Le Cesarine is a network of home cooks in hundreds of towns. Book a meal or a cooking class in someone's kitchen: hand-rolled pasta in Emilia, orecchiette in Puglia, Sunday ragù in Naples. You eat what you made, with a glass of the local wine.
items.meta: Meals and classes, usually 3 to 4 hours

image.alt: Trays of handmade orecchiette and other pasta outside a doorway in Bari's old town
image.credit: Maddy16869, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Markets, cellars and supper clubs
items.subtitle: Campagna Amica, Cantine Aperte, Eatwith
items.desc: Shop where Italians shop: Campagna Amica farmers' markets sell straight from the producer, and the town market is the best free show in any city. On Cantine Aperte weekend in late May, hundreds of wineries open their doors. For dinner with strangers who become friends, Eatwith lists meals hosted in private homes.
items.meta: Markets are busiest on Saturday mornings

image.alt: A farmers' market stall with pumpkins, vegetables and local produce
image.credit: Anna.Massini, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: How to blend in
sections.intro: Italians are forgiving of visitors, but these habits will win you warmer smiles.

items.title: Greet everyone
items.desc: Say buongiorno when you walk into a shop, bar or lift, and buonasera from late afternoon. Arrivederci on the way out. Ciao is for friends.

items.title: Cover up in churches
items.desc: Shoulders and knees covered, hats off, voices low. Big churches such as St Peter's turn people away, so carry a light scarf. Do not wander around during Mass.

items.title: Keep beachwear for the beach
items.desc: Walking through town in swimwear or bare-chested is frowned on, and several resorts, from Sorrento to Capri, fine it.

items.title: Eat on Italian time
items.desc: Lunch is roughly 12:30 to 14:30, dinner from 19:30 in the north and 20:30 or later in the south. Many kitchens close between services, so a 16:00 lunch may mean a sandwich.

items.title: Drink coffee like a local
items.desc: Un caffè is an espresso, drunk standing at the bar in a minute. Cappuccino is a morning drink. In busy bars you pay at the till first, then hand your receipt to the barista.

items.title: Join the passeggiata
items.desc: From about 18:00, towns stroll the main street or seafront, dressed a little better than you would expect. Join in, then stop for an aperitivo: a spritz or a glass of wine with snacks.

items.title: Respect the afternoon pause
items.desc: In small towns and the south, many shops close from about 13:00 to 16:00 or later, and Sunday is quiet. Plan errands for the morning or early evening.

items.title: Keep the peace at home
items.desc: Apartment buildings expect quiet in the early afternoon and from about 22:00 to 8:00. Sort your rubbish by the building's recycling calendar; your host will explain it.

items.title: Ask for the bill
items.desc: Lingering is the point, so the bill will not arrive until you ask: il conto, per favore. Paying alla romana means splitting it evenly.

items.title: Treat monuments gently
items.desc: Do not sit or eat on church steps and famous monuments, wade in fountains or picnic on Venice's bridges. Rome, Florence and Venice issue fines.

items.title: Find the end of the queue
items.desc: At a busy bakery or market stall, ask chi è l'ultimo? (who is last?) and you will know your turn. Delis often use paper tickets.

items.title: Learn ten words
items.desc: Per favore, grazie, scusi, permesso (excuse me, coming through) and a cheerful buongiorno open doors. Even a clumsy attempt is appreciated.

tips: Italian law requires every host, hotel or private, to register your passport details with the police; this is normal.
Tourist tax is charged per person per night almost everywhere, including in agriturismi and rentals, and is often paid in cash on arrival.
Many agriturismi and masserie set a minimum stay of two or three nights, or a full week in August.
Rifugi and farm stays in remote areas may not take cards; carry enough cash.
If a rental listing has no CIN code, or the host asks you to pay off-platform by bank transfer, walk away.
